title: Speaking practice: Reasons, Data, and Daily Life
description: Eight speaking tasks. Students explain melting ice, argue for a stop sign and a water station, sort a school day into before and after lunch, summarize a text, explain a math strategy, use ramp data, and retell a town history. Students record two takes; teachers or students review the recordings.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Mina put two ice cubes of the same size on two plates. She put one plate in the sun and one plate in the shade. After 10 minutes, the ice cube in the sun was a small puddle. The ice cube in the shade was still mostly ice.
Tell your partner why the two ice cubes looked different after 10 minutes.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your neighborhood is deciding whether to put a new stop sign on Maple Street. You are speaking at the neighborhood meeting. Here are some facts.
Many children walk on Maple Street to get to school.
Cars often drive fast on Maple Street.
There is no stop sign on Maple Street now.
A stop sign makes cars wait, so a car trip can take a little longer.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A new student named Sofia joins your class today. She wants to know what the day will be like. Use this schedule to tell Sofia which things happen before lunch and which happen after lunch.
8:30 Morning meeting
9:00 Reading
10:15 Recess
11:00 Math
12:00 Lunch
1:00 Science or art
2:30 Pack up and go home
Then tell Sofia which part of the day you like best and why.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Read this short text. Then tell a friend what it is mostly about.

An octopus is a sea animal with a soft body and eight arms. It has no bones, so it can squeeze through very small spaces. An octopus also has three hearts. Many octopuses can change the color of their skin to match rocks or sand, which helps them hide from enemies.
Use your own words. Do not read the text word for word.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A school hall has 4 rows of chairs. Each row has 6 chairs. A student says there are 24 chairs in all.
Your partner is not sure the answer is right. Show your partner two different ways to find the number of chairs. Say your math steps out loud.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: You are speaking to the principal at a school meeting. You want the school to add a water-bottle filling station in the second-floor hallway. Here are the facts you collected.
About 140 students on the second floor bring a reusable water bottle to school.
There is only one drinking fountain on that floor.
At lunch time, a line of 12 students waits at the fountain.
The principal says, “A new station costs money.” Answer this worry in your talk.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Dara tested a toy car on a ramp. She used the same car and the same floor each time. She changed only the height of the ramp. At each height, she rolled the car three times and wrote down the average distance.
Ramp height 10 cm: the car rolled 80 cm.
Ramp height 20 cm: the car rolled 150 cm.
Ramp height 30 cm: the car rolled 210 cm.
Dara says, “A higher ramp makes the car roll farther.” Tell your science group whether the data support her claim.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A visiting student is doing a project about libraries. Read this short history of the made-up town of Willow Creek. Then tell the visitor how the town got its library.

Long ago, the town of Willow Creek had no library. In 1952, a teacher named Mr. Alvarez asked each family to give one book. Neighbors brought more than 300 books in wagons and wheelbarrows. They put the books in an empty barn. Volunteers painted shelves and sorted the books by topic. On opening day, 200 people came to borrow books. Today the old barn is still the town's library.

items.stem: Explain why the ice cube in the sun melted faster than the ice cube in the shade.

checklist: I told what happened to each ice cube.
I used the word because to give a reason.
I said how the sun and the shade were different.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: describes both results and gives a reason that links warmth from the sun to faster melting.
Organization: states the result first, then the cause.
Sentence-level language: at least one because or so clause connecting cause to effect.
Vocabulary: words such as melt, warm, sun, and shade used accurately.

support.clue: Notice where each plate was and how much ice is left on each plate. Think about what the sun gives to things it shines on.
support.frame: The ice cube in the ______ melted faster because ______. In the shade, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About wet clothes: “A wet T-shirt on a clothesline dried in 30 minutes on a warm, windy day. A wet T-shirt in a cool closet was still wet the next day. The T-shirt outside dried faster because the warm moving air took the water away.” Now explain why the ice cubes were different.

facts: Ice melts when it gets warmer.
Things in direct sunlight usually get warmer than things in the shade.

items.stem: Tell your neighbors whether Maple Street should get a stop sign, and give a reason.

checklist: I said yes or no to the stop sign.
I gave one or two reasons.
I used a fact about Maple Street.
I used because to connect my reason to my choice.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: gives a clear yes or no and at least one reason based on the facts.
Evidence: uses a fact from the prompt (children walking, fast cars, or the longer trip) rather than only saying it is a good idea.
Sentence-level language: because or so to connect reason and claim; simple sentences that are mostly accurate.
Clarity: speaks clearly enough for a neighborhood audience.

support.clue: Look at the four facts. Think about who walks on the street and how the cars drive. What could a stop sign change, good or not so good?
support.frame: I think Maple Street ______ get a stop sign because ______. Also, ______. A stop sign can ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a park: “I think the park should have more trash cans because we see litter on the grass. Also, many families eat picnics there. More trash cans can help keep the park clean.” Now say what you think about the stop sign.

items.stem: Tell Sofia which things happen before lunch and which happen after lunch. Then tell which part of the day you like best.

checklist: I told what happens before lunch.
I told what happens after lunch.
I used words like before lunch and after lunch.
I said which part I like best and gave a reason.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: sorts the schedule accurately into before lunch and after lunch and names at least four items.
Organization: tells one group first and then the other, and ends with a personal choice.
Vocabulary: names subjects and routines (reading, recess, math, science) correctly.
Sentence-level language: present-tense statements (we have, we go), group words (before, after), and because for the reason.

support.clue: Find lunch on the schedule. Put the lines above it in one group and the lines below it in another group. Then pick one line you like.
support.frame: Before lunch, we ______, ______, and ______. After lunch, we ______ and ______. I like ______ best because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a park: “Some things in the park are for playing and some are for resting. The swings, the slide, and the soccer field are for playing. The benches and the picnic tables are for resting. I like the swings best because I can go high.” Now tell Sofia about your school day in the same way.

items.stem: Tell a friend the main idea of the text about octopuses and give two important details.

checklist: I told the main idea in one sentence.
I gave two details that support the main idea.
I used my own words and did not read the text word for word.
I used a linking phrase like for example or also.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states a main idea that covers the whole text (the octopus has body features that help it live and stay safe) and gives two accurate details.
Organization: main idea first, then details, then a closing sentence.
Vocabulary: uses words such as soft body, arms, hearts, and hide accurately or paraphrases them.
Sentence-level language: noun groups (a sea animal with eight arms) and linking words (also, for example).

support.clue: Read the text once. Ask: what is every sentence about? Then choose two facts that show it.
support.frame: The text is mostly about ______. One important detail is ______. Another detail is ______. This shows that ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a different animal: “The text is mostly about how camels live in the desert. One important detail is that camels can go many days without drinking water. Another detail is that their wide feet help them walk on sand. This shows that camels have body parts for desert life.” Now give the main idea and two details about the octopus.

facts: Many octopuses can change skin color to blend in with their surroundings.

items.stem: Show your partner two different ways to find how many chairs are in 4 rows of 6 chairs.

checklist: I explained the first way step by step.
I explained a second way that is different.
I said the total each time.
I used words like rows, each, and altogether.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: explains two different, valid strategies (for example, 6 + 6 + 6 + 6; 4 × 6; or 2 rows is 12 so 4 rows is 24) and reaches 24 both times.
Mathematical reasoning: each step is correct and states the intermediate numbers.
Organization: first way, then second way, then a comparison or closing statement.
Vocabulary: rows, each, altogether, multiply or add, and equal groups used accurately.

support.clue: Think about at least two ways to combine equal groups. Could you add, multiply, or double?
support.frame: One way is to ______. That gives ______. Another way is to ______. Both ways give ______, so ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About bags of oranges: “There are 5 bags with 2 oranges in each bag. One way is to draw 5 groups of 2 and count them: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Another way is to multiply: 5 × 2 = 10. Both ways give 10, so there are 10 oranges.” Now show two ways to find the number of chairs.

items.stem: Persuade the principal to add a water-bottle filling station to the second-floor hallway.

checklist: I clearly asked for what I want.
I gave two reasons that use the facts.
I answered the principal's worry about money.
I used polite, strong language (I believe, I respectfully ask).
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states a clear request, supports it with two reasons from the facts, and responds to the cost worry.
Evidence: uses specific numbers (140 students, one fountain, line of 12).
Organization: request, reasons, answer to the worry, and a closing sentence.
Sentence-level language: complex sentences with although, since, or even if for the counter-argument; audience-appropriate polite tone.
Elaboration: explains why the station would help beyond restating the facts, for example less waiting and healthier habits.

support.clue: Count the facts. Which facts show that there is a problem? Think about what the principal worries about.
support.frame: I am asking you to ______ because ______. First, ______. Second, ______. Some people may say ______, but ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a bike rack: “I am asking you to add a bike rack near the front gate because many students ride to school. First, bikes now lean against the fence and fall over. Second, students lock their bikes in different places, so the walkway is blocked. Some people may say there is no room, but the grass beside the gate is empty.” Now make your request about the water station.

items.stem: Use Dara's data to explain whether a higher ramp makes the toy car roll farther.

checklist: I said whether the data support Dara's claim.
I used at least two numbers from Dara’s data.
I said that only the ramp height changed.
I used a comparing phrase like as the ramp got higher, the car rolled farther.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states that the data support the claim and explains why.
Evidence: cites at least two data points and notices the pattern across all three heights (80, 150, 210 cm).
Scientific reasoning: notes that the car and floor stayed the same, so the ramp height is the likely reason.
Sentence-level language: comparison and pattern language (as ... increased, the farther, compared with).
Vocabulary: terms such as height, distance, data, and claim used accurately.

support.clue: Look at the numbers going down the list. What happens to the distance each time the height goes up? What stayed the same?
support.frame: Dara's claim ______ supported by the data. When the ramp was ______ cm high, the car rolled ______ cm. When the ramp was ______ cm high, it rolled ______ cm. This pattern shows that ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About dissolving sugar: “Hana says that warmer water dissolves sugar faster. She used three identical cups, the same amount of water, and one spoonful of sugar in each. In her table, 20 °C water took 60 seconds, 40 °C water took 35 seconds, and 60 °C water took 20 seconds. The data support her claim because the warmer the water was, the less time the sugar needed. Only the water temperature changed.” Now judge Dara’s claim.

facts: In the test, the distance rolled was 80 cm at 10 cm height, 150 cm at 20 cm height, and 210 cm at 30 cm height.
In a fair test only one thing is changed at a time.

items.stem: Retell the story of how the town of Willow Creek got its library, in the order it happened.

checklist: I told the events in the order they happened.
I used time words such as first, then, after that, and today.
I used past-tense verbs for the events in 1952.
I said who did what (the teacher, the neighbors, the volunteers).
exemplar: Task fulfilment: retells the main events (the request for books, the donations, the barn, the shelves, opening day, today) in order.
Organization: opening that sets the problem (no library), middle events, and an ending that connects to today.
Sentence-level language: past tense for the history and present tense for today; time words and phrases.
Elaboration: includes specific details such as the number of books or the neighbors' wagons.
Clarity: uses the names and groups from the history (Mr. Alvarez, neighbors, volunteers) without confusing who did what.

support.clue: Find the time words in the history (long ago, in 1952, on opening day, today). They show the order. Notice who does each thing.
support.frame: Long ago, ______. Then, ______. After that, ______. Next, ______. On opening day, ______. Today, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a school garden: “Long ago, the school yard was only grass. Then a class asked the principal for a garden. After that, parents dug the soil. Next, students planted seeds and watered them. On the first harvest day, the class shared carrots with the school. Today the garden is still growing.” Now retell the history of the Willow Creek library.
